e-470.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
e-470.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2 = (3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \,\textrm d u=\textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{4\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{12}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-471.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
e-471.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \dfrac{3}{2 + 50x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{3}{2(1 + 25x^2)} = \dfrac 3 2 \int \dfrac{1}{1+25x^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+u^2}\textrm{d}u =\arctan u +C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $25x^2 = (5x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 5\,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2+50{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-5014.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
e-5014.worked_solution:
This resembles the basic integral for $\textrm{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

Let $u = 5x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
5\,\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\,\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(5x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-472.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions
e-472.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+{x}^{2}/2)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this integral now resembles the basic integral for the inverse tangent,

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\,\textrm d u = \arctan{u} + C.
$$

We make the substitution $u=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt 2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡u|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $81{x}^{2}=(9x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=9x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9\sqrt{1-81{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(9x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(9x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate ∫191−81x2dx.

a
81arcsin⁡(9x)+C
b
19arcsin⁡(x)+C
c
181arcsin⁡(9x)+C
d
9arcsin⁡(9x)+C
e
19arcsin⁡(9x)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, ∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 81x2=(9x)2.

So, let's substitute u=9x. Differentiating, we get dudx=9⟹dx=19du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫191−81x2dx=19∫11−(9x)2dx=19∫11−u2⋅(19du)=181∫11−u2du=181arcsin⁡u+C=181arcsin⁡(9x)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $81{x}^{2}=(9x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=9x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9\sqrt{1-81{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(9x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(9x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{\sqrt{1-3{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{\sqrt{1-(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.

$$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫41−2x2dx.

a
22arcsin⁡(2x)+C
b
22arcsin⁡(2x)+C
c
2arcsin⁡(2x)+C
d
2arcsin⁡(2x)+C
e
2arcsin⁡(x)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, ∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 2x2=(2x)2.

So, let's substitute u=2x. Differentiating, we get dudx=2⟹dx=12du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫41−2x2dx=4∫11−(2x)2dx=4∫11−u2⋅(12du)=42∫11−u2du=422arcsin⁡u+C=22arcsin⁡(2x)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $2{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $36{x}^{2}=(6x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{6\sqrt{1-36{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(6x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{36}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{36}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(6x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)}{2}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

∫11−4x2dx=

a
arccos⁡(2x)2+C
b
arcsin⁡(2x)2+C
c
arccos⁡(4x)4+C
d
2arcsin⁡(2x)+C
e
arcsin⁡(4x)4+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 4x2=(2x)2.

So, let's substitute u=2x. Differentiating, we get dudx=2⟹dx=12du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate:

∫11−4x2dx=∫11−(2x)2dx=∫11−u2⋅(12du)=12∫11−u2du=12arcsin⁡u+C=arcsin⁡(2x)2+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)}{2}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{25+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{25\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/25)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/25}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/5)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{25+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/5)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as follows: ∫125+x2dx=∫125⋅(1+x2/25)dx=125∫11+x2/25dx=125∫11+(x/5)2dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent ∫11+u2du=arctan⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x5)2.

So, let's substitute u=x5. Differentiating, we get dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫125+x2dx=125∫11+(x/5)2dx=125∫11+u2⋅(5du)=15∫du1+u2=15arctan⁡u+C=15arctan⁡(x5)+C

decision.explanation: Let u=5x, so dx=du/5. The integral becomes (1/5)∫du/(1+u²)=arctan(5x)/5+C, matching option c.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5x)}{5}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫11+u2du=arctan⁡u+C.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5x)}{5}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent, ∫11+u2du=arctan⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 16x2=(4x)2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(4x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x/8, so dx=8 du and 64+x²=64(1+u²). The integral becomes (1/4)∫du/(1+u²)=arctan(x/8)/4+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{64+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2}{64\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/64)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{64}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/64}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/8)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{8})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{8}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=8\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{64+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{32}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/8)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (8\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{8})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{8})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{8}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=8\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{9}{81\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/81)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/81}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

 The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{9})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{9}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{9}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=9\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (9\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as follows: ∫981+x2dx=∫981⋅(1+x2/81)dx=19∫11+x2/81dx=19∫11+(x/9)2dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent ∫11+u2du=arctan⁡u+C. The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x9)2.

So, let's substitute u=x9. Differentiating, we get dudx=19⟹dx=9du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫981+x2dx=19∫11+(x/9)2dx=19∫11+u2⋅(9du)=∫du1+u2=arctan⁡u+C=arctan⁡(x9)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{9}{81\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/81)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/81}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

 The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{9})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{9}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{9}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=9\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (9\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{3\,\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}=3\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $9x.$

So, let's substitute $u=9x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{3\,\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}=3\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $9x.$

So, let's substitute $u=9x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3\int \frac{1}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(9x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{5}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{5}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{5}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫dx|x|5x2−1=∫5|5x|(5x)2−1dx.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 5x.

So, let's substitute u=5x. Differentiating, we get dudx=5⟹dx=15du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫1|x|5x2−1dx=∫5|5x|(5x)2−1dx=5∫1|u|u2−1⋅(15du)=5⋅15∫du|u|u2−1=arcsec u+C=arcsec(5x)+C

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{4|x|\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|4x|\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $4x.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4|x|\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|4x|\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫14|x|16x2−1dx=

a
arcsec(16x)2+C
b
4arcsec(4x)+C
c

d
arcsin⁡(4x)4+C

arcsec(4x)4+C

Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫dx4|x|16x2−1=∫dx|4x|(4x)2−1.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 4x.

So, let's substitute u=4x. Differentiating, we get dudx=4⟹dx=14du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫14|x|16x2−1dx=∫1|4x|(4x)2−1dx=∫1|u|u2−1⋅(14du)=14∫du|u|u2−1=14arcsec u+C=arcsec(4x)4+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{4|x|\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|4x|\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $4x.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4|x|\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|4x|\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=√2 x. Then dx=du/√2 and |x|=|u|/√2, so these factors cancel. The integral becomes ∫du/(|u|√(u²−1))=arcsec(√2 x)+C, matching option e.

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{2}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

Question 14
?

Calculate ∫1|x|2x2−1dx.

a
2arcsec(2x)+C
b
2arcsec(2x)+C
c
2arcsec(x)+C
d
arcsec(x2)+C
e
arcsec(2x)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫dx|x|2x2−1=∫2|2x|(2x)2−1dx.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 2x.

So, let's substitute u=2x. Differentiating, we get dudx=2⟹dx=12du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫1|x|2x2−1dx=∫2|2x|(2x)2−1dx=2∫1|u|u2−1⋅(12du)=2⋅12∫du|u|u2−1=arcsec u+C=arcsec(2x)+C

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e. Substituting u=√2 x cancels the scale factors, giving arcsec(√2 x)+C. Its derivative is 1/(|x|√(2x²−1)), the original integrand.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{2}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{2}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6|x|\sqrt{36{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x|\sqrt{(6x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $6x.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{6|x|\sqrt{36{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|6x|\sqrt{(6x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(6x)}{6}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫dx6|x|36x2−1=∫dx|6x|(6x)2−1.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 6x.

So, let's substitute u=6x. Differentiating, we get dudx=6⟹dx=16du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫16|x|36x2−1dx=∫1|6x|(6x)2−1dx=∫1|u|u2−1⋅(16du)=16∫du|u|u2−1=16arcsec u+C=arcsec(6x)6+C

decision.explanation: Rewrite the denominator as 2(1+(2x)²). With u=2x, dx=du/2 and the limits become 0 and 14. Thus the integral is (9/4)[arctan(u)]₀¹⁴=(9/4)arctan(14), matching option c.

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{9}{2+8{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $14$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{9}{2+8{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{14}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{\int }_{0}^{14}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{14} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(14)-\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(14)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{16\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/16)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can write this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{20}{3+75{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{20}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{20}{3+75{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{20}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{20}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$
